slide.title: Test Before You Build
slide.body: Mock-up of a one-page landing page with one button: 'Join the waitlist'. Small target icon labelled 'Threshold'. Small tag: Building an AI Startup · Lesson 4.

scenes.voiceover: Interviews tell you that a problem is real. They do not tell you whether people will act: sign up, give their time, or pay. You can find out in a few days, before you build anything.

slide.title: Testing Demand Before You Build
slide.body: Building an AI Startup · Lesson 4 of 15

scenes.voiceover: In the last lesson, you learned to interview customers. Now we test whether they will do something. A demand test is a small, cheap experiment that asks people to take a real action. Actions are stronger evidence than words.

slide.title: Test 1: Landing page
slide.body: Simple one-page mock-up: headline naming the problem, two lines of text, one button 'Join the waitlist' → arrow → list of email sign-ups.

scenes.voiceover: The first test is a landing page. That is a single web page that describes your product and asks visitors to do one thing, such as leave their email to join a waitlist. You can make one with Canva or a free no-code builder. If people will not even leave an email, they are unlikely to pay later.

slide.title: Tests 2 and 3
slide.body: Left: Concierge test: you deliver by hand; customer knows a person does it. Right: Wizard of Oz test: looks like a product; a person does the AI's job behind a curtain. Footer: be honest, no false promises.

scenes.voiceover: The second is a concierge test. You deliver the service yourself, by hand, and the customer knows a person is doing it. The third is a Wizard of Oz test. The customer uses what looks like a product, but a person does the AI's job behind the scenes. Be honest if customers ask, and never promise automation you cannot deliver.

slide.title: Success threshold
slide.body: 'If at least 20 of 100 visitors join the waitlist, we continue.' Below: conversion rate = 20 ÷ 100 = 20%. Tag: written BEFORE the test.

scenes.voiceover: Before any test, write a success threshold, the result that counts as a yes. For example, if at least twenty of one hundred visitors join the waitlist, we continue. That is a conversion rate of twenty percent: the share of people who take the action. Set the number before the test, so you cannot change your mind later.

slide.title: Evidence ladder
slide.body: Ladder from bottom to top: Like → Email address → Time on a call → Deposit or pre-order → Paid order (top, strongest).

scenes.voiceover: Stronger actions give stronger evidence. From weakest to strongest: a like on social media, an email address, time on a call, a small deposit or pre order, and finally a paid order.

scenes.stock_query: chef serving guests at pop up dinner
scenes.voiceover: Think of a chef before a restaurant opens. She runs a few pop up evenings in a borrowed kitchen. She does not buy the building first. If people come, pay and return, she has evidence. If the tables are empty, she has lost a few evenings, not her savings.

scenes.stock_query: teenager doing maths homework at home evening
scenes.voiceover: Let's look at an example. Hamza is a made up founder in Lahore, Pakistan. He believes parents of secondary school students want affordable evening help with maths homework. His long term idea is an AI tutor on the phone that explains problems in Urdu or English.

slide.title: Hamza's landing page
slide.body: Mock-up page: 'Send a photo of a maths problem before 9 p.m. and get a step-by-step explanation in 30 minutes.' Button: 'Send a problem'.

scenes.voiceover: But he does not build anything. He runs a concierge test. He makes a flyer and a simple landing page. Send a photo of a maths problem before nine in the evening, and get a step by step explanation in thirty minutes.

slide.title: Threshold, written first
slide.body: In 2 weeks: at least 15 families send a problem · at least 5 agree to pay a small weekly fee for week 3 · shared in parent groups at two schools

scenes.voiceover: Before he shares it, he writes his threshold. In two weeks, at least fifteen families send a problem, and at least five agree to pay a small weekly fee for a third week. Then he shares the page in parent groups at two schools.

scenes.stock_query: two people writing maths explanations at table
scenes.on_screen_text: No AI yet. Done by hand.
scenes.voiceover: When photos arrive, Hamza and a friend who teaches maths write the explanations by hand. There is no AI yet, only people doing the job.

slide.title: Result vs threshold
slide.body: Target 15 families → actual 22 (green tick). Target 5 paying → actual 7 (green tick). Learned: requests 8–9 p.m. · voice notes preferred · geometry diagrams hardest.

scenes.voiceover: After two weeks, twenty two families have sent problems, and seven have agreed to pay. The threshold is met. He also learns three things he could not have guessed. Most requests arrive between eight and nine in the evening. Parents prefer voice notes. And geometry problems with diagrams are the hardest.

A common mistake is deciding what success means after you see the numbers. A weak result suddenly becomes a promising start. Write the threshold down and share it first. And share your page with your real target group, not only friends and family.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Real actions beat opinions. 2. Landing page, concierge, Wizard of Oz. 3. Threshold first; real target group.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, demand tests ask people for a real action, which is stronger evidence than an opinion. Second, landing pages, concierge tests and Wizard of Oz tests let you learn before you build the AI part. Third, set your threshold before the test, and share it with your real target group.

Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, build a one page landing page with Canva or a no-code builder, write your success threshold, and share it with at least ten people in your target group. Next, we ask a hard question: is it defensible? See you there.
